post1.text:
Most companies scaling past $50M don't have a strategy problem. They have a leadership problem they've mislabeled as strategy.

When organizations expand their executive teams specifically to handle growth, as we're seeing more companies do across industries from healthcare to tech, the instinct is to hire for function. Hire a COO. Add a VP of Sales. Bring in a Chief of Staff. But the leaders who actually move the needle at this stage share one trait that no org chart captures: they lead as if real consequences are on the line every single day.

Here's what that looks like in practice:

1. They make decisions at speed without waiting for consensus that will never come.
2. They hold accountability up, not just down. Senior leaders answer to the same standards they set for their teams.
3. They treat culture as an operational input, not a values poster on the wall.

At the $50M to $500M inflection point, leadership stops being about inspiration and starts being about results. The organizations that scale successfully know the difference.

What's the leadership behavior your company rewards that it shouldn't?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Stanford Graduate School of Business makes a sharp point: before scaling AI across an organization, executives need to genuinely understand what they're scaling into, not just what they're scaling up.

This matters enormously for companies in the $50M to $500M growth corridor. At that stage, the temptation is to adopt every tool that promises efficiency. But technology scales your existing leadership and decision-making, for better or worse. If your processes are broken, AI makes them faster and more broken.

The real competitive advantage isn't adoption. It's the leadership clarity to know which problems you're actually solving before you deploy any solution at scale.

post3.text:
When Strive Health expanded its executive team specifically to scale value-based kidney care, they made a bet that growth requires the right leadership infrastructure, not just more capital or more customers.

That bet is exactly what Chapter 1 of Rock Your Business addresses. The chapter, titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It, was written by Katherine Slain and opens with a premise that stops most scaling leaders cold: at this stage of growth, the quality of your leadership is no longer a soft consideration. It is the variable that determines whether your business survives the climb from $50M to $500M.

Katherine lays out what it actually means to lead with that level of urgency and accountability, and why most executive teams operating at scale are still leading like they did at $10M.

The insight is uncomfortable. That's exactly the point.

post1.text:
Most business owners think they build value and then plan their exit. That sequence is backwards, and it costs them millions.

Your multiple is not determined at closing. It is determined years before you ever sit across from a buyer. J.P. Morgan's private bank research on exit strategies reinforces this: the decisions you make while running the business are the decisions that set your price.

Here is what $50M+ leaders need to understand:

1. Buyers pay premiums for predictability. Recurring revenue, documented processes, and low owner dependency compress perceived risk and expand your multiple.

2. Your EBITDA number matters less than your EBITDA story. Buyers are purchasing future cash flow, not past performance. How you frame trajectory changes offers.

3. Optionality is leverage. Owners who enter a process with multiple strategic and financial buyers at the table consistently outperform those who pursue a single path.

The window to maximize your multiple is open right now, not when you decide you are ready to sell.

What is the single biggest factor you believe drives your company's valuation today?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes on exit planning breaks down the essential elements owners need to get right before a transaction. It is worth a read, but here is what it does not say loudly enough: most mid-market companies between $50M and $500M treat exit planning as a finish line activity instead of an operating discipline.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this gap constantly. By the time a founder is ready to sell, value leakage has already happened. Talent dependencies, customer concentration, and weak financial reporting are not problems you fix in a six-month sprint before going to market.

If you are running a company at scale, exit readiness is a growth strategy, not an endgame. Start building for it now.

Read the Forbes piece here and then ask yourself whether your business is buyer-ready today: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPQjFIYXhibGVtZGsyVmtwMGZpTjdobTVlcEJOMURid0JybUZzRjlzc212dU85c29LdEFYMXJDRU1vNzYtVXZIZzFhZVU4T3RpdzZ5VnR2bkZ2ZXJPRG83d1hiTFJ4UF85WHR5QnNJc0wzdEdqS0xsQXdFVi1JeG0zSGxYY3ZtX1ZUYkxWaDRpcE9sTENEVlNuN1pKTkxzZmRyOGc

post3.text:
Exit planning conversations are everywhere right now. Forbes, J.P. Morgan, industry roundtables. Everyone agrees it matters. Far fewer people explain exactly how to do it at scale.

That is what Chapter 2 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles directly. The chapter is titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, and it was written by Paul Belair and George Hohman, two practitioners who have worked inside these transactions at the $50M to $500M level.

One thing they make clear: there is a specific set of value drivers that sophisticated buyers weight heavily, and most owners are not actively managing them. Knowing what those drivers are changes how you run your business today, not just how you negotiate tomorrow.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most owners assume their exit multiple is a reward for past performance. It is not. It is a bet buyers are making on your future, and they price that bet based on what they see inside your business right now. If you are running a company between $50M and $500M, the gap between your current multiple and your potential multiple is almost always a leadership and operations problem, not a market problem.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M+ don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. Habits are what your team does because that's what they've always done. Strategy is a deliberate set of choices about who you sell to, how you win, and what you stop doing.

Gartner recently found that the AI time savings sales teams are gaining won't translate into revenue unless leadership steps in to redirect that capacity toward the right activities. That's not an AI problem. That's a strategy problem.

Here's what scaling companies get wrong:

1. They confuse revenue growth with a working sales strategy. The two are not the same.
2. They let top reps define the process by default, which means the process only works for that rep.
3. They never define what a qualified opportunity actually looks like at their stage of growth.

If your sales team is busy but your pipeline is unpredictable, you don't have a strategy problem. You have a clarity problem.

What does your sales process actually optimize for?

post2.text:
A recent piece from McKinsey on the economics of B2B growth makes something very clear: the threshold for survival has moved. Companies that used to coast on mid-single-digit growth are now genuinely at risk.

At Autobahn, we see this play out with scaling companies every year. Growth that felt safe at $50M becomes fragile at $150M if the sales engine underneath it was never built to hold the weight.

The McKinsey data reinforces what we tell our clients: revenue at scale is not a sales effort problem. It is a sales architecture problem. The companies that thrive are the ones that build strategy before they desperately need it.

If your sales motion was designed for the company you were, it may be working against the company you are trying to become. Read the full piece here and then ask yourself whether your strategy is built for where you are going.

A recent report found that B2B sales teams now need AI and personalization just to stay competitive. That is a real shift. But here is what the headlines miss: technology does not fix a broken sales strategy. It accelerates whatever you already have in place.

Chapter 4 of our upcoming book Rock Your Business, titled Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation, addresses exactly this. Authors Deb and Brandon lay out why companies between $50M and $500M are the most vulnerable to this trap. They are big enough to have real sales complexity but often still running on the informal playbook that got them to this stage.

One thing the chapter makes clear: if you cannot write down your sales strategy in plain language, you probably do not have one yet.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they walk away from an interaction with your company.

Most $50M+ leaders treat branding as a design problem. It is actually a sensory and cultural problem. JBL figured this out. Instead of running campaigns, they built their marketing around the spaces and communities where their customers actually live. The result is a brand that feels like it belongs, rather than one that interrupts.

Here is what that means for scaling companies:

First, your brand needs a point of view that survives without a budget behind it. If it disappears when you stop spending, it was never a brand.

Second, consistency across channels is not about repeating a message. It is about evoking the same feeling whether someone reads your website, talks to your sales team, or opens your invoice.

Third, culture eats campaigns for breakfast at scale. The companies winning long-term are building identity, not awareness.

So, what feeling does your brand actually leave behind?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive featuring Ulta's CMO caught our attention. The core idea was straightforward: brand building and performance marketing are not opposing forces. They are a system, and the best operators run them together.

For companies scaling past $50M, this matters more than most leaders realize. At that stage, it becomes tempting to chase short-term channel performance while the brand slowly loses coherence. Ulta's approach is a reminder that omnichannel is not a distribution strategy. It is a brand consistency strategy.

If your customer experience feels different depending on where they find you, your brand is working against your growth, not for it.

Read the full piece and ask yourself: does your marketing infrastructure support a unified brand, or is it fragmenting one?

Campari has spent decades managing a portfolio of iconic brands across wildly different cultures, occasions, and audiences. A recent ADWEEK feature explored how they do it without losing what makes each brand distinct. The answer is disciplined brand stewardship, not creative reinvention.

That tension is exactly what Chapter 5 of Rock Your Business tackles. The chapter, titled What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?, was authored by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West. Their insight is that growing companies rarely fail because of bad marketing execution. They fail because leadership has never defined what the brand is actually supposed to feel like at scale.

Before you build a campaign, you need to be able to answer that question. Simpson and West show you how.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost problem disguised as momentum.

SHRM's latest research on 2026 hiring trends confirms what we see with scaling companies every day: the leaders who win are not the ones adding headcount fastest. They are the ones who have stopped treating recruiting like a volume game and started treating it like a precision operation.

Here is what that means in practice for companies in the $50M to $500M range:

1. Every open role should have a clear performance outcome attached before the job post goes live. Not a list of duties. An outcome.

2. Your best candidates are evaluating you as hard as you are evaluating them. Your hiring process is a preview of your culture.

3. Retention starts at the offer stage. If you are not explicit about what success looks like in year one, you are setting people up to leave.

Growth at this stage is not about having enough people. It is about having the right ones in the right seats, moving in the same direction.

What is the one hiring assumption your leadership team has never actually tested?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM on 2026 hiring trends made something very clear: precision is replacing scale as the defining principle of talent acquisition.

For companies in growth mode, this is not a trend to watch. It is a decision to make now.

At Autobahn, we work with leadership teams navigating the $50M to $500M range, and the ones who stall almost always have the same problem: they scaled their headcount without scaling their standards. They hired for availability instead of alignment.

Precision hiring means knowing exactly what a role needs to produce, who is built to produce it, and how your process filters for that. It is slower upfront and far less expensive over time.

If your recruiting process was built when you were a $20M company, it is time to rebuild it.

Read the full SHRM piece here and bring it to your next leadership conversation: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMioAFBVV95cUxPRFVYR0VscXJpMmVqV2dwazJDTkstVDJTNG9uTlZlWHJPVkFqQ0MzZTRQSUYwUDZweWw2dE52THZKSnhBTzQtb1g5UUYzbmJTbjFJcXlVYno2ZzU4aE0yNVRwN2RIN05xTWJVWnZQejVyY2xRNmJ2SF83QmVHel9GYmdWTEdEMWZLMVk5OThMNTF0TmdKR1F4bG84cnZRZ0FU?oc=5

post3.text:
The conversation around precision hiring is not new to us. It is the foundation of Chapter 6 in our upcoming book.

In Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond, Chapter 6 is called The Talent Engine. It was written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West, three practitioners who have worked inside the people challenges that scaling companies actually face.

One thing Chapter 6 makes clear: talent strategy at this stage of growth is an operational system, not an HR function. The companies that scale well have built a repeatable engine for finding, developing, and keeping the right people. The ones that stall are still running on instinct and gut feel.

There is a specific framework in this chapter that reframes how leadership teams think about role design before a search ever begins. We will be sharing more soon.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better decisions. They make more meetings.

Most companies scaling past $50M fall into the same trap: they add metrics every quarter and call it accountability. What they have built is a dashboard nobody trusts and a leadership team that spends more time explaining numbers than acting on them.

Oracle NetSuite recently published a list of 30 financial metrics companies should track heading into 2026. Thirty. For a scaling business, that kind of breadth is not a strategy. It is noise with a spreadsheet attached.

Here is what actually works at the $50M to $500M stage:

First, every KPI should connect directly to a decision someone is authorized to make. If no one owns the outcome, the metric is decorative.

Second, when your leadership team cannot recite your top five metrics from memory, you have too many.

Third, lagging indicators tell you what happened. Scaling companies need leading indicators that tell them what is about to happen.

How many of your current KPIs would survive a hard audit this quarter?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Oracle NetSuite lays out 30 financial metrics and KPIs companies should consider tracking in 2026. It is a thorough list and genuinely useful for teams building their measurement infrastructure.

But here is what the article does not address: for companies in active growth mode, the volume of metrics is often the problem, not the solution.

At Autobahn, we work with leadership teams scaling from $50M to $500M and beyond. The pattern we see repeatedly is not a lack of data. It is a lack of clarity about which numbers actually drive the business forward. More metrics create more reporting cycles and fewer decisions.

If your team is revisiting its KPI stack heading into the back half of the year, start by asking which metrics you would keep if you could only keep five.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMikwFBVV95cUxNcThuZllxNkVka0dpOV9QdHZQM2RiU0tfMGVIR05tdW9ZN1AtYngwQ1d4WDFSb3ZNSUxKNHFCSUR4aC1lR1g2ZWYzWFE0NWF1WmVpejAxOW9VRFdJa01yLUFKa1hvbjNGQnR6a2hZcVVtQzgwRXNCdXVGbjhfNWR2eWpTSlFyRk5zLVZ3MnJvMU14ZjA

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that every operations leader at a scaling company needs to read before they build their next dashboard.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business is titled Death by KPIs. It was written by Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, three practitioners who have sat inside the chaos that comes when a growing company confuses measurement with management.

The chapter tackles something most KPI articles will not say directly: tracking more metrics does not create more accountability. At a certain point, it creates the opposite. Leaders get buried in reporting and lose the thread of what actually moves the business.

One idea from this chapter worth sitting with is that the right number of KPIs is not determined by your industry. It is determined by the decision-making capacity of your leadership team.

Rock Your Business, the second book from Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, is available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
AI will not save your business. Your strategy around AI will.

There is a critical difference, and most executives at the $50M to $500M growth stage are missing it. They are buying tools. They are not building systems.

Bloomberg recently surveyed twelve CEOs on how they actually use AI day to day. The takeaway is not about any single tool. It is about intentional integration into decision-making and delegation workflows.

Here is what that means for scaling companies:

First, AI amplifies your existing operational clarity. If your processes are unclear, AI makes the chaos faster.

Second, the leaders seeing real productivity gains are using AI to extend their thinking, not replace it. They are making better decisions in less time.

Third, AI adoption without accountability structures creates a false sense of progress. Output increases. Outcomes do not.

The companies that scale past $100M are not the ones with the most AI tools. They are the ones who know exactly why each tool is there.

So the real question is: does your team use AI with intention, or just convenience?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Newsweek asked a question that every executive at a growing company should be sitting with: AI is boosting productivity, but is it actually worth it?

At Autobahn Consultants, we work with companies scaling from $50M to $500M. And we see this tension constantly. Leaders adopt AI, output goes up, but margins, clarity, and team alignment do not always follow.

Here is our angle: productivity gains without strategic alignment are just faster noise. The companies we see winning with AI are the ones treating it as a leadership decision, not an IT decision.

If you are evaluating AI investments at your company right now, this article is worth your time. Read it, then ask your leadership team one honest question: what problem are we actually solving?

post3.text:
The New York Times recently covered executives using AI twins to manage their time and extend their reach. It sounds futuristic. It is actually a sign of something much more practical: the best leaders are rethinking how they show up and where they spend their attention.

Chapter 8 of Rock Your Business, titled The Third Monitor Theory, tackles exactly this. Co-authored by Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain, the chapter introduces a framework for how scaling company leaders should be integrating AI into their daily operating rhythm, not as a gadget, but as a core part of how they lead.

One thing the chapter makes clear: the leaders who benefit most from AI are the ones who have already done the hard work of knowing their priorities. AI does not create focus. It rewards it.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to derail a scaling company are not the ones who lack confidence. They are the ones who fake having it.

Imposter syndrome does not disappear when you hit $50M in revenue. Forbes Australia recently reported that high achievers carry it straight to the top, and in many cases it intensifies as the stakes rise. That detail matters more than most leadership conversations acknowledge.

Here is what scaling leaders need to understand:

First, imposter syndrome in a CEO or senior leader does not stay private. It leaks into decisions, specifically in the form of over-delegation, avoidance of bold moves, and approval-seeking from boards or peers who expect conviction.

Second, the leaders who scale successfully are not the ones who eliminated self-doubt. They are the ones who stopped letting it sit in the driver's seat.

Third, recognizing the syndrome in yourself is not weakness. Ignoring it while running a $200M organization absolutely is.

So here is the question worth sitting with: If your company is growing but your leadership identity is not, which one do you think wins?

post2.text:
A recent piece from Seattle University outlined six practical ways leaders can overcome imposter syndrome when stepping into a new leadership role. The advice is solid for individuals. But it stops short of addressing what actually happens inside a scaling company.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. A leader who managed well at $30M gets promoted into a $100M operation and suddenly second-guesses every decision. The problem is not competence. It is identity lag, the gap between who they were and who the role now demands.

For companies pushing past $50M, that lag is expensive. It slows decisions, shrinks risk tolerance, and creates culture drift at the top.

If your leadership team is scaling faster than their confidence, that is a business problem, not a personal one. Let's talk about how to close that gap.

Chapter 9 of our forthcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?" and it tackles something most business books skip entirely: what happens to a leader's psychology when the company outgrows their previous identity.

Coauthored by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo, the chapter goes beyond naming imposter syndrome and gets into the specific patterns that surface in $50M to $500M organizations. One of the most striking insights is that imposter syndrome at this level rarely looks like self-doubt. It looks like over-control, perfectionism, and an inability to build a leadership team you actually trust.

If your company is scaling but something feels off at the top, this chapter was written for that moment.

post1.text:
Most $50M+ executives treat life planning like a retirement activity. That is a costly mistake.

Work-life design is not a reward you earn after scaling. It is a strategic input that determines whether you survive the scaling process at all.

Morgan Stanley recently published research on what happens to founders after a liquidity event. The pattern is striking: leaders who had no identity or structure outside the business struggled far more than those who had intentionally built a life alongside it.

Here is what high-performing leaders at this stage actually do differently:

1. They define what winning looks like personally before they define it operationally.

2. They protect recovery time the same way they protect board meetings. It is non-negotiable.

3. They audit their calendar quarterly, not just their P&L.

The business will demand everything you give it. The question is whether you decide in advance what you are unwilling to give.

What would you find if you audited your last 90 days?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune from Morgan Stanley lays out what life looks like for entrepreneurs after selling their business, and the roadmap they share is worth reading whether an exit is years away or already on the table.

Here is what stood out to us at Autobahn: most founders at the $50M to $500M growth stage are so focused on the next operational milestone that they give zero thought to who they are outside of the company they are building.

That gap does not just create post-exit regret. It creates leadership fragility right now, during the years when clear-headed decision-making matters most.

If you are scaling a business and have not asked yourself what a well-designed life actually looks like for you, this article is a good place to start.

post3.text:
Morgan Stanley's recent work on life after a business exit surfaces a question that most scaling executives never think to ask until it is too late: what are you actually building toward?

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, tackles this head-on. Authored by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain, this chapter is one of the most honest in the book.

The insight that will stop you mid-read: the leaders who scale fastest are not the ones who sacrifice everything. They are the ones who design their life with the same rigor they apply to their business model.

Most executives at this growth stage have never done that work. This chapter shows you where to start.

posts.blog_hook: Somewhere between $50M and $500M, most executives quietly lose the thread of their own life. The business becomes the identity, the calendar becomes the plan, and recovery becomes a foreign concept. The leaders who actually make it through that growth stage intact have something in common: they treat life design as a business discipline, not an afterthought.
